t: Find the Sum of the Power of All Subsequences
o: Sum, over all 2^n subsequences S of nums, the number of sub-subsequences of S whose elements sum to k. Rephrasing as a triple count: pick a 'core' set B with sum k, then every element outside B may freely be in or out of the enclosing subsequence, contributing 2^(n−|B|) enclosing subsequences. Hence the answer is Σ over subsets B with sum k of 2^(n−|B|). Example: nums=[1,2,3], k=3 gives cores {1,2} (weight 2) and {3} (weight 4) → 6. With n ≤ 100 and k ≤ 100, a knapsack DP indexed by (sum, cardinality) fits easily; elements larger than k can be discarded.
k: Swap the summation order: answer = Σ_{B: sum(B)=k} 2^(n−|B|), counting each (enclosing subsequence, core) pair once.
A 2D knapsack dp[count][sum] counts subsets by size and sum; elements > k are irrelevant.
Multiply each dp[c][k] by 2^(n−c) and sum to get the answer.

a.i: Process elements one at a time, keeping a table dp[c][s] = number of subsets of the processed prefix with c elements and sum s. Each new element either joins a subset or not; copying the table per layer keeps the reasoning simple.
s: For each element x ≤ k, create the next table adding dp[c][s−x] into dp[c+1][s] for all valid c, s.
a.t: O(n² · k) — three nested loops over elements, counts, and sums (≤ 100·100·100).
a.sp: O(n · k) for the DP table.

a.i: The same transition can be done in place by iterating the count dimension downward: when updating dp[c+1][s] from dp[c][s−x], the source row c has not yet been modified in this element's pass, so no copies are needed.
s: Keep a single dp[c][s] table initialized with dp[0][0] = 1.
For each x ≤ k, loop c from high to low and s from k down to x, adding dp[c][s−x] into dp[c+1][s].
Finish with the weighted sum over column k.
a.t: O(n² · k) — same triple loop without table copies.
a.sp: O(n · k) for the single DP table.

w: Lead with the counting reversal — it converts an intimidating sum-of-powers into a standard knapsack. Pitfalls: forgetting to skip elements larger than k (they only waste time, never correctness), and forgetting the 2^(n−c) weight (which encodes the free outer elements). Edge cases: k unreachable gives 0 naturally; duplicate values are handled because cores are index sets. Follow-up: what if the power counted sub-arrays instead of sub-sequences, or if k were up to 10^4 (bitset-accelerated knapsack).
